claim: Design each dashboard within the BI extension's limits: aggregate data, up to 50,000 rows a query and a 30-day default range.
problem: Aggregate-only queries and the 50,000-row maximum are real limits. The 30-day range is not: the BI extension needs a date range in each query and uses the last 30 days when none is given, but a query can set any range with the timestamp or daterange columns. Calling it a limit to design within (here, and in the risk line '... and the 30-day default range before building') tells executives who compare web and sales totals over months and quarters that their dashboards stop at 30 days. The row figure also needs care: when a query sets no LIMIT, the default is 50 rows.
evidence_quote: The BI extension requires a date range to limit the rows used for calculations. The default is the last 30 days, but you can override this in your SQL WHERE clause using the special timestamp or daterange columns.
fix: 'Design each dashboard within the BI extension's rules: aggregate queries only, a row limit of up to 50,000 a query (the default is 50 when a query sets none), and an explicit date range in every query, since without one the extension reads only the last 30 days.' Risk line: 'Dashboards that break the BI extension's rules: we design for aggregate queries, a row limit of up to 50,000 and an explicit date range in each query before building.'

verdict.reason:
The finding survives. I tried to refute it four ways:

1. The auditor's quote is word for word on Adobe's BI extension page. It sits under "Defaults and limitations", which opens: "The following additional defaults and limitations apply when using the BI Extension".
2. Adobe does group defaults with limits there, and the answer does say "default". But the answer lists the 30-day range among "the BI extension's limits" and twice says the dashboards are designed "within" it: in How we would do it, and in the risk line ("we design within ... the 30-day default range"). Read plainly, that means the dashboards stay inside 30 days. Adobe says the default can be overridden with the timestamp or daterange columns.
3. I looked for a real cap and found none:
   - Adobe's own Power BI Desktop example covers a whole year. The Monthly trend use case (experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/analytics-platform/using/cja-usecases/data-views/bi-extension/monthly-trend) "shows a monthly trend of occurrence (events) for 2023", with the filter "on or after 1/1/2023 And is before 1/1/2024".
   - The Limits use case filters Power BI to "the last 1 calendar years".
   - The CJA guardrails page (technotes/guardrails) lists no date-range cap for ad-hoc SQL queries. Its only date-range limit is Report Builder's 13 months.
4. For this client it is also a misfit. Vennor's executives already use Power BI and dispute web against sales totals, which they will compare over months and quarters. The right design rule is an explicit date range in every query: a visual with no range silently returns only the last 30 days (Adobe's Monthly trend page first shows "the occurrences for the current month" before the filter is set). That mismatch is exactly the kind of gap these executives already dispute.

The aggregate-query and "up to 50,000 rows a query" parts are correct. Leaving out the 50-row default is an omission, not an error. Adobe's guardrails page lists 50,000 as the "Default number of rows returned unless specified otherwise" for ad-hoc SQL. That conflicts with the BI extension page's default of 50, so the fix should cite the BI extension page for the 50 or drop it. The finding holds on the 30-day point.
verdict.evidence_quote: The BI extension requires a date range to limit the rows used for calculations. The default is the last 30 days, but you can override this in your SQL WHERE clause using the special timestamp or daterange columns.
